source_evidence.observation: The integral conservation law is d/dt ∫[x₁,x₂] q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)). Each component of q measures the density of a conserved quantity; its total amount between the endpoints changes only through endpoint flux.

source_evidence.location: Raw PDF page 26, printed page 4, §1.1.2; raw PDF page 27, printed page 5, continuation
source_evidence.anchor: provided that q and f(q) are sufficiently smooth; integral conservation law (1.10) is the more fundamental equation
source_evidence.observation: Sufficient smoothness permits deriving differential equation (1.8) from (1.10). Solutions can contain discontinuities, including shock waves, and nonlinear conservation laws can develop discontinuities from smooth initial data. At a discontinuity the differential equation does not hold classically, while the integral conservation law continues to hold.

contract_plain_english: The integral conservation law balances the change of the conserved state integrated over an interval against its endpoint fluxes (printed p. 4, (1.10)). This remains fundamental for discontinuous solutions, where the differential equation fails classically (printed pp. 4–5, §1.1.2). Finite volume methods approximate integrals over grid cells, or cell averages obtained by dividing those integrals by cell volumes, and update them through numerical edge fluxes based on the available approximate averages (printed p. 5, §1.2). Given averages Q_{i−1} and Q_i in neighboring cells, use them as the left and right constant states of a Riemann problem for the hyperbolic equation. Solving that problem supplies information usable to compute a numerical flux and update cell averages over a time step (printed p. 5, §1.2.1, (1.11) and following paragraph). The passage leaves the information representation, flux formula, update formula, and value of the initial state at the jump unspecified. It also recognizes approximate Riemann solvers in numerical implementations (printed p. 6, §1.2.1).
